Triggers.value: Being in a locked or confined room

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I tell myself the event did not really happen or was not that bad
I dwell on what I have done wrong
I go over and over the details of the event trying to make sense of it

Threat.value: I feel on guard even inside my own home
I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong

Negative Appraisals.value: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable.
You can never know who will harm you

vignette:
Marisol Fuentes is a 59-year-old divorced Latina woman who has worked as a project manager for a mid-sized construction firm for nearly two decades. She presents with a PCL-5 score of 77, seeking help approximately fourteen months after an experience of captivity that she describes, even now, in fragments - sometimes minimizing it entirely in one breath and then weeping through the details in the next.

The incident occurred during what began as a routine site visit to a facility under renovation. A dispute between contractors escalated into a confrontation, and Marisol found herself locked inside a small, windowless site office by a man she had managed professionally for over a year. She was held there for several hours. During that time, she had no phone signal, the door handle would not turn from the inside, and when she screamed, the noise of the construction work swallowed her voice. At one point he returned, stood in the doorway, and grabbed her by the back of the neck - hard enough that she felt the pain for days afterward and was later found to have a mild soft tissue injury. She was ultimately found by another worker who noticed the door had been wedged shut from the outside. She has never described the full sequence of events to anyone in its entirety.

In the weeks that followed, Marisol told herself it had not been that bad - that she had overreacted, that nothing truly terrible had happened. She returned to work within days, which she now recognizes as consistent with a version of herself she no longer fully inhabits. But the minimizing did not hold. She began going over the hours in that room repeatedly, reconstructing each moment, searching for the point at which she could have acted differently, spoken differently, managed the situation as the competent professional she had always been. She was certain she had missed something - a warning sign, a moment of weakness in her own judgment - and she dwelt on this with an intensity that consumed her evenings.

Her work as a project manager requires her to conduct walkthroughs of active sites, attend coordination meetings in temporary site offices, and occasionally travel to facilities mid-renovation. These settings have become quietly agonizing. When she enters a room and hears the click of a door closing behind her, something in her body responds before her mind can intervene. Windowless conference rooms, portable site offices, even the small bathroom on her office floor - any space that registers as enclosed and lockable pulls at something she cannot fully name. She has begun arriving at meetings early so she can position herself nearest the door, and she has declined two site visits in the past quarter by citing scheduling conflicts, a pattern her supervisor has begun to notice. The professional consequences are accumulating in ways she cannot entirely conceal.

At home, Marisol does not feel safe in the way she once did. She sleeps with the bedroom door open and checks the locks on her front door several times each night, not because she believes someone is outside, but because something in her nervous system refuses to be persuaded otherwise. She cannot settle into an evening - cannot read, cannot watch television without her attention sliding toward the sounds of the building. Her body remains faintly braced, as though waiting for something she cannot name to arrive. When her neck aches - as it does in cold weather, or after a long day at her desk - the pain carries a quality that ordinary muscle tension does not. It lands differently, and she finds herself somewhere else entirely for a moment before she returns.

What frightens Marisol most is not the memory itself but what she has come to believe about the world and about herself. She had always considered herself someone who read people accurately and moved through life with competence and warmth. Now she holds a quiet, settled conviction that anyone, at any moment, might be capable of harm - that the categories of safe and unsafe no longer apply in the way she once trusted them to. She describes feeling dead inside in a way that puzzles and distresses her, as though the woman who used to find genuine pleasure in her work and her relationships has become inaccessible. It was her daughter, noticing the withdrawal over a family visit at Christmas, who finally asked her directly whether she was all right. Marisol had no answer she could give. She made the appointment the following week. What she is most hoping for, she says quietly, is to feel like herself again - though she is not entirely sure she still knows who that is.
